column1: ## When to use

The rule that does all the work: **ask within 24 hours of the compliment — never later.** ""That's amazing, thank you!!"" in your inbox is a perishable asset. Most agencies say ""thanks"" and move on; the disciplined one converts gratitude into proof within a day.
## The ask (make it effortless — effort kills testimonials)
Never ""could you write us a testimonial?"" (blank page = never happens). Give structure:
> Hi [NAME] — that just made my week, thank you.
> Since you're happy (and only because you are): would you put a few words in writing? Three prompts, answer any or all, rough is perfect:
> 1. What was going on before we started? (the ""before"")
> 2. What did we do that stood out — working style counts as much as the work?
> 3. What's the result you'd point to? Numbers welcome, honesty over precision.
> Two lines per answer is plenty. If it's easier, reply in bullets and I'll shape a draft for your approval — you edit anything, nothing goes public without your sign-off.
> And to be clear: a ""not now"" costs nothing. [NAME]
The **draft-for-edit** route converts best: busy clients approve-and-tweak; they don't compose.
## Shaping what they send back
- **Keep their words.** Light edits for length and typos only — polished marketing-speak reads fake and they'll notice their voice missing.

- **Anchor specifics:** ""great to work with"" is worthless; ""they caught that our checkout was losing mobile sales — recovered about $4k/month"" is a weapon. If their draft is vague, one follow-up: *""Could you add the number that made you happiest? Even rough.""*
- **Collect permissions explicitly:** full name, title, company, photo, and where it may appear (website, proposals, social). Log the permission date next to the quote.
- **Quote bank:** one file/table — quote, who, permission, where used. Every proposal (SOP-03 §6) pulls from it; every listing too.
## From testimonial to case study (within 30 days, best projects only)

Structure (one page): **Before** (their words from the discovery notes, SOP-02) → **What we did** (3–5 moves, outcome-worded) → **The number** (their metric from SOP-07, before/after) → **Their quote** (the shaped testimonial) → **What it took** (timeline + price range if they permit — price ranges pre-qualify your future leads, SOP-01 bonus).
## Copy-paste: the 30-day follow-up (if they went quiet)

> Hi [NAME] — no rush and no pressure on the words from last month; your inbox is a war zone, I get it. If it's easier, just reply with the one number you'd brag about from [PROJECT] and one sentence why — I'll draft around it as before. If it's a no, we're completely good, and [RESULT] was a blast either way.
## Rules & red flags
- One nudge only, ~30 days later. A second chase converts goodwill into a favor they resent — the exact opposite of the asset's purpose.
- Never write a fake testimonial or ghost-write one they don't edit. It's dishonest, it leaks, and clients talk.
- Fresh testimonials beat old ones: rotate the two quotes in proposals (SOP-03 §6) quarterly; an agency whose newest proof is 3 years old is telling on itself.
- The testimonial conversation is also the natural door to SOP-23 (referrals): the thank-you email after they approve the quote adds the ""one small favor"" — the referral ask.
## What good looks like
- 60%+ of happy clients provide a usable quote within a week (the 3-prompt + draft-for-edit format gets you there; the blank ""any chance you could…"" request doesn't).
- Every proposal carries a quote from the last 2 quarters, with a number in it.
- One case study per quarter enters the quote bank — your listing pages (Gumroad/Etsy/website) and SOP-01 nurture emails feed on these forever.
## Adapt it with AI

> ""Write my testimonial request email for [SERVICE] clients: 3 prompts tailored to what my work changes for [NICHE], plus the draft-for-edit line. Then turn this raw client feedback into 2 polished-but-in-their-voice quotes and one case study using the Before/Did/Number/Quote structure: [PASTE FEEDBACK + METRICS]."""
SOP-23 · Alumni Referral Program,"Offboarding","# SOP-23 · Alumni Referral Program

column3: Handover complete (SOP-21) · testimonial approved (SOP-22) · quarterly value email cycle
10 minutes at handover · 1 hour per quarter maintaining
A referral engine made of people who already know your work — the cheapest, warmest pipeline a small agency can own

column1: ## When to use

At every project close and then once a quarter, forever. Past clients (""alumni"") refer more freely than current ones — the project's results are proven, and recommending you costs them nothing but a forward. Most agencies never ask because the project ""ended."" That's the entire opportunity: for the client, the relationship didn't end; the *invoice* did.
## Copy-paste: the referral ask (at handover + testimonial approval, two separate asks)
The referral ask is distinct from the testimonial ask — never bundle them into one email with two favors (you'll get neither):
> Hi [NAME] — one more thing now that [PROJECT] is wrapped, and it's a good one: **who else do you know with the [PROBLEM YOU SOLVED] problem?**

> Not asking you to sell for me — one name and a ""you two should talk"" is the whole job. I'll take it from there with zero awkwardness (they'll get value from the first call whether we work together or not).
> If someone comes to mind, a one-line intro by email is perfect. And thank you — [RESULT] was a pleasure.
## The forwardable blurb (give them the ammunition)
People refer when it's effortless. Attach a 60-word blurb they can forward untouched:

> *Forwarding this because [YOUR NAME] did [SPECIFIC RESULT, e.g., ""our site rebuild — leads up 40% in 3 months""] for us. [HE/SHE/THEY] run(s) [AGENCY], working with [NICHE] on [SERVICES]. First call is genuinely useful even if you don't hire — [HE/SHE/THEY] does a teardown of your [ASSET] with no strings. [YOUR EMAIL / CALENDAR LINK]*
Refresh the blurb's headline number quarterly (newest case study, SOP-22). A stale number is a stale pipeline.
## The thank-you (always, same week)
> Hi [NAME] — [REFERRAL NAME] and I just talked; great human, exactly the kind of project I like. Thank you for the intro.

> Small token: [REFERRAL THANK-YOU — e.g., ""the next [X] hours on any future project for you are on me"" / a gift / a donation they'd like]. No obligation ever attaches to this — the intro was the gift.

**Check the rules of your jurisdiction and their industry** before offering cash commissions (some regulated industries and government clients forbid it); a gift, discount, or free hours is the safe universal default.
## The alumni rhythm (1 hour per quarter)
1. **List:** every past client in one sheet: name, project, last result, last contact date.
2. **One value email per quarter** — no pitch: the new case study, one insight useful to *their* business, one line of ""door's open"" (this doubles as SOP-24's nurture bed).

3. **Three personal touches per quarter:** congratulate a launch, comment on their news, send a relevant article *they* specifically would use. alumni ≠ mailing list; alumni = 30 humans who know your work.
4. **Annual audit:** who referred in the last 12 months? Thank them again (differently). Who went quiet 18+ months? They're SOP-24 candidates now.
## Rules & red flags
- Ask at the *high point* (handover, testimonial, results call) — never during a low, and never more than once per project cycle.

- Treat referred leads like royalty, visibly: faster SLA on the first reply (SOP-01 fast-track), and report back to the referrer *with their permission to share progress* — referrers who see outcomes refer twice.
- Never let a referred project go badly without telling the referrer first. Protect the referral triangle's trust above the single project's revenue.
- Don't pay for referrals where it's prohibited (regulated industries, public sector) and always keep it transparent — sleazy referral economics eventually reach the client's ears.
## What good looks like
- 25%+ of new business arriving by referral within a year of running this rhythm (it starts slower; compounds fast).
- Every quarter: one alumni email sent, three personal touches logged, blurb number refreshed.
- The phrase ""I heard about you from [PAST CLIENT]"" — arriving monthly — is this SOP compounding.
## Adapt it with AI

> ""Write my referral ask, my 60-word forwardable blurb (latest result: [NUMBER/PROJECT]), and my quarterly alumni email for [NICHE] past clients. My referral thank-you is [GIFT/DISCOUNT/HOURS]. Warm, zero-pressure tone — these people liked working with me; the emails should feel like me, not a newsletter."""
SOP-24 · Win-Back Sequence,"Offboarding","# SOP-24 · Win-Back Sequence

column3: 90+ days since project end, no retainer, no active conversation — and the account scored 🟢/🟡 when it ended
20 minutes per touch × 3 touches, spaced ~6 weeks
Reactivated clients — or a clean archive after 3 touches, with the relationship intact for SOP-23 referrals

column1: ## When to use

On the alumni list (SOP-23 rhythm) whenever an account goes quiet. Win-back is slower than referral but warmer than cold outreach: these people already know your work. The entire game is *patience + relevance* — three touches over ~18 weeks, each carrying something useful, never ""just checking in.""
## The sequence (spaced ~6 weeks)

column4: Content
One insight specific to *their* business/market (""saw [INDUSTRY THING] — this changes [THEIR ASSET] because…""). No offer, no ask beyond ""worth a look?""
Your newest case study (SOP-22) with a one-line bridge: ""similar setup to yours — [NUMBER] in [TIMEFRAME].""
The direct email below — a specific idea for their business and an easy way in.

column1: ## Copy-paste: the three emails
**Touch 1 — value:**

> Hi [NAME] — no agenda, saw [SOMETHING SPECIFIC: their launch / an industry shift / a competitor move] and thought of you: [2–3 SENTENCE INSIGHT that connects it to their business]. Might be useful, might not — seemed worth sending either way. How's [THEIR WORLD — e.g., the new store] treating you?
**Touch 2 — proof:**

> Hi [NAME] — we just closed [PROJECT] for a [SIMILAR PROFILE] client: [ONE NUMBER RESULT] in [TIMEFRAME]. Wrote it up here ([LINK], 2-minute read) — the middle section on [TOPIC] applies almost word-for-word to your [THEIR ASSET]. Anyway — no ask, just figured you'd find it interesting.
**Touch 3 — direct:**

> Hi [NAME] — last one from me for a while (not a guilt trip, just file-closing honesty): I keep having ideas for [THEIR BUSINESS] — the current one is [SPECIFIC IDEA, one sentence, tied to something you can see]. If it's interesting, reply and I'll shape it into a one-pager with a price range, no commitment. If the timing's wrong, reply ""not now"" and I'll check back next quarter — and either way, [GENUINE WISH — e.g., ""hope the expansion's going great""].

Then act on the reply taxonomy: **""not now""** → archive to the quarterly alumni email (SOP-23), revisit in 2 quarters · **""maybe""** → book a 20-minute call, smallest next step (SOP-18 grammar) · **silence** → archive. Silence *is* an answer, and honoring it is what keeps the door unlocked for next year.
## Stop conditions (hard rules)
- **Explicit no, or a competitor signed** → archive immediately, congratulate them on the competitor signing if you hear (seriously — it's remembered).
- **Two full sequences with zero replies** → this account is an alumni-email-only account now. A third sequence isn't persistence; it's the reason people mute senders.
- **The ending was ugly** (fired mid-project, payment fight) → no sequence. One apology-and-clean-slate email if you owe one (SOP-21 grace rules), then referral-grade distance.
## Rules & red flags
- Every touch must be *about them*: an insight, a proof point, a specific idea. The moment a touch is about your pipeline targets, it reads as such and burns a cycle.
- Personalize from public signals (their site, their LinkedIn, their industry news) — five minutes of homework per touch. A win-back you could have sent to anyone will be archived by everyone.
- Space the touches; three emails in three weeks is pressure, not presence. ~6 weeks apart, ≤ 3 touches, then rest for at least 2 quarters.
- Log everything in the alumni sheet: touch dates, angles used, replies. After two quarters you'll know which angle (value/proof/direct) wakes your kind of clients — lead with that one next cycle.
## What good looks like
- 10–20% of sequenced accounts re-engage within a year (small numbers, huge margin: these close in one call, no discovery-from-zero).
- Every re-engagement starts with their reply, never with your discount. Leading with a discount teaches alumni your prices were padding all along (SOP-04 rule holds here hardest).
- The alumni sheet never has an account sitting in ""should probably email them sometime"" — it's in a sequence, in the quarterly email pool, or archived. Three states, no limbo.
## Adapt it with AI

> ""Write my 3-touch win-back sequence for [NICHE] alumni clients. Touch 1 must reference something checkable on their website/LinkedIn; touch 2 bridges my best case study ([SUMMARY]); touch 3 proposes [IDEA TYPE]. My voice: [SAMPLE]. Add a 're-engaged' first-call agenda — these people skip discovery basics, so the call needs its own shape."""
